title: From Good to Great to Built to Last
hook: A trophy case can become a warning label if the habits behind it stop being practiced.
counterintuition: Most leaders treat a leap as an ending because visible success feels like proof. Lasting strength requires the same disciplines after the win, when pride makes truth, focus, and standards harder to protect. The paradox is that the less dramatic move often protects the stronger result.
tryThisNow: Pick one recent win and write the habit that produced it. Schedule one action this week that protects that habit instead of celebrating the win again.
keyTakeaway: A leap becomes lasting only when the institution keeps practicing the disciplines that created it, especially after success makes comfort and pride easier to justify.

undefined.

Linda faces the same pattern in another setting, with a different object on the table and the same pressure to make the comfortable choice. The details change, but the discipline stays plain.

A good organization can drift because each small compromise looks reasonable. One softened fact, one wrong seat, one attractive side path, one tool bought from fear, one reset made too soon. None of these choices announces itself as a collapse.

The better move is to force the standard into the open while the choice is still live. keep practicing the disciplines that created the win after success arrives. Once the standard is visible, people can argue with it, improve it, or accept its cost.

A second scene makes the lesson travel. Someone at home, in a clinic, on a loading dock, or in a classroom can use the same test without using business language. The point is not the setting. The point is the discipline under pressure.

There is a limit. A standard can become rigid if people stop checking facts. A focus can become pride if it refuses new evidence. The safeguard is plain contact with the real situation in front of you.

The final test is whether the next action leaves the system stronger. If it only feels easier, louder, or more flattering, it probably belongs outside the work that makes greatness last.

You can run the same test outside a company. A parent can use it before relaxing a rule that created trust. A nurse can use it before smoothing a number that needs action. A student can use it before joining one more club that steals time from the work that matters. The setting changes, but the pressure is familiar: something easy asks to be treated as wise.

The answer is to slow down just enough to name the source of strength. Then choose the next action that protects that source. If the action feels quieter than a dramatic reset, that is fine. The point is not to impress the room. The point is to leave the system stronger after the room empties.

questions.prompt: A manager faces a live choice around From Good to Great to Built to Last. Which move best applies the idea? The decision is due before lunch, the team has one whiteboard marker left, and everyone can see the tempting shortcut on the table.
choices: Use the clear test: keep practicing the disciplines that created the win after success arrives
Pick the action that looks boldest in the meeting
Wait for pressure to pass before naming a standard
questions.explanation: The disciplined move uses the core test while the choice is still live. Boldness and delay can both hide the real issue.

questions.prompt: A team is tempted by a good-looking option that does not fit the chosen standard. What should happen first? The proposal looks useful, but two people in the room have already noticed that it pulls time away from the work that created the recent gain.
choices: Approve it because a good option should not be wasted
Test it against the standard and say no or reshape it
Ask the newest person to decide so politics stay low
questions.explanation: A good-looking option can still scatter force. The standard should decide before social pressure takes over.

questions.prompt: If you are coaching someone through this idea, which prompt is strongest? The person you are coaching has five minutes before a committee vote and needs a question that turns the idea into a real test.
choices: Who will get credit if this works?
How can we make this feel more exciting?
What evidence would prove this choice strengthens the system?
questions.explanation: The best coaching prompt turns the idea into evidence and system strength, not emotion or credit.

questions.prompt: A person wants to soften a hard fact because morale is fragile. Which response fits best? The team is tired, morale is thin, and a soft phrase would let the meeting end without naming the fact everyone can see.
choices: Name the fact plainly and connect it to the next action
Hide the fact until morale improves
Replace the fact with a hopeful story
questions.explanation: Plain truth tied to action protects morale better than evasion. People can handle reality when it is usable.

questions.prompt: A group has one scarce hour before a decision. What is the best use of that hour? The clock on the wall says 4:40 p.m., and the group has one hour before the budget window closes.
choices: Practice the announcement
Clarify the one standard that will govern the choice
Collect more options without judging any
questions.explanation: The hour should make the decision cleaner. More options or a better announcement can wait until the standard is clear.

questions.prompt: Someone says the disciplined choice feels less impressive. Which answer is most accurate? The quieter choice will be harder to explain because it does not look like a launch, a rescue, or a bold public turn.
choices: Impressive is always the wrong goal
Less impressive choices are always safer
The right choice may look quieter because it protects compounding strength
questions.explanation: The point is not to avoid impressive moves. The point is to protect the pattern that can keep building.

questions.prompt: A team repeats the same mistake after praise or pressure changes the mood. Which intervention is best? The mistake happened after praise changed the mood, and the team is starting to treat the old habit as optional.
choices: Return to the habit or standard that produced the earlier strength
Add three new priorities to renew energy
Avoid talking about the mistake so people stay positive
questions.explanation: The strongest intervention reconnects the team to the source of strength before drift becomes normal.

questions.prompt: A leader is unsure whether a new tool, person, or project belongs. Which question should decide? The new option has a vendor demo, a confident owner, and a real price tag, but fit is still unclear.
choices: Will this be easy to defend politically?
Does this reinforce the system we are trying to build?
Can this make us look current by Friday?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement is the useful test. Politics and appearance may matter, but they cannot decide the fit.

questions.prompt: Which personal-life transfer is strongest? The same pattern has started showing up at home: too many options, not enough protection for the habit that was working.
choices: Change goals whenever motivation dips
Treat every opportunity as a yes
Name the core habit and remove one attractive distraction
questions.explanation: The same lesson transfers to personal work: protect the repeatable source of strength and cut what scatters it.

reviewCards.front: A choice looks attractive but may scatter effort. What do you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the governing standard first, then test the choice against it before pressure or excitement sets the answer.

reviewCards.front: A room wants a louder move. What should you teach back?
reviewCards.back: Loud moves only help when they reinforce the system. Quiet moves can be stronger when they keep force pointed in one direction.

reviewCards.front: A win or crisis is changing behavior. What is the hard retrieval question?
reviewCards.back: Ask which habit, fact, person, or focus created strength, then protect that source before adding anything new.

reviewCards.front: A pressured room wants the comfortable answer. Which move should come back first?
reviewCards.back: Bring the decision back to the visible standard and the next concrete action. Comfort can be considered only after the standard has been named.

reviewCards.front: A strong result is making the team relax. What should you retrieve before drift starts?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the source of the result: the person, fact, focus, habit, or repeated push that created strength. Protect that source before adding anything new.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is turning From Good to Great to Built to Last into a concrete test at the moment of choice. You name what must be protected, then choose the action that strengthens the system instead of the action that merely feels safe or dramatic.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work decision starts to sprawl, then write the governing standard in one sentence before voting or replying.
If a health plan gets crowded, then keep the repeatable habit and cut one add-on that only creates noise.
If a personal project gets praised or pressured, then protect the practice that produced the progress.
If a relationship improves after a hard talk, then repeat the small behavior that made truth safer instead of assuming the win will last.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, apply From Good to Great to Built to Last to one live choice. Write the tempting move, the governing standard, and the next action that protects the source of strength.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review three choices and mark each as reinforcing, resetting, or drifting. Keep one reinforcing action and cut one drifting action.

memorableLines.text: A trophy case can become a warning label if the habits behind it stop being practiced.
memorableLines.why: Opens the idea through a concrete, surprising image that reverses what success means.

memorableLines.text: A good organization can drift because each small compromise looks reasonable. One softened fact, one wrong seat, one attractive side path, one tool bought from fear, one reset made too soon. None of these choices announces itself as a collapse.
memorableLines.why: The specificity of the list makes drift tangible—each mistake is named, so none can hide as small.

memorableLines.text: The point is not to impress the room. The point is to leave the system stronger after the room empties.
memorableLines.why: It's the chapter's actual punchline—a decision rule that reverses the instinct to perform rather than protect.
